extracted.intended_audience: architects, students of architecture, designers, and architectural critics
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive aesthetic guidance for designing and judging architecture with emphasis on power, scale, materials, and the proper relation of ornament to structure. Covers choices of form, masonry, surface treatment, repetition, and the moral/ stylistic integrity of a building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and unity of mouldings
rubrics_metrics.description: Mouldings and prominent junctions should be managed with perfect simplicity; avoid introducing different mouldings merely to obtain variety of intersectional line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of good practice: the junctions in the triforium of Salisbury are kept in the shade and use mouldings like each other. Anti-pattern: late builders who fix attention on lines rather than enclosed spaces, leading to studious association of different mouldings and discordant intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional moulding sizes for grouped shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Moulding dimensions must be appropriate to the size of each shaft; smaller shafts require smaller moulding proportions and independent bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Where smaller shafts are grouped with larger ones, give each shaft an independent base proportioned to its scale; calculate points of emergence 'with the utmost nicety' so smaller bases appear as if formed within larger ones (example: nave of Abbeville).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical precision and craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections and joins should be calculated and cut with singular precision; fine details may be so slight as to be perceptible mainly by touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibit technical dexterity: 'the strangest possible shapes of sections being calculated to a hair's-breadth.' Complex examples require measured sections to be intelligible (figures cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive intersectional ornament and involution
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow mouldings and forms to be multiplied and bent through themselves to the point of caricature and incoherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include mouldings carried thrice through themselves, ends cut off when unmanageable, flattened arches, shrunken pillars, lifeless ornament, liny moulding, distorted foliation. Such excess betrays a 'fallacious system' and leads to loss of unity and principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve integrity and obedience to architectural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture must obey its own laws and preserve a single truth of its order, consistency, and organization; abandoning this integrity leads to decay of the style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin's warning: the loss of 'its own truth' caused Gothic to sink; the error of zeal or luxury dissolves strength. Moral/ stylistic fidelity is a criterion of sound architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two intellectual Lamps: gathering (veneration) and governing (dominion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The architect must know what to gather from nature (veneration of natural forms) and how to rule or govern those materials with human intellect; these are the two great intellectual principles of architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architecture shows man 'either as gathering or governing'; success depends on knowing which natural forms to emulate and how to impose human order upon them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of abstract power and majesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture should aim, where appropriate, to express a severe and mysterious majesty — an 'abstract power' akin to great spiritual forces — not merely prettiness or ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This faculty differs from mere invention or proportion; aim to mark man's relation with the mightiest works of Nature (cliffs, mountains, seas) and to achieve sublimity through that sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisive choice of scale: prioritize size or decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether a building's principal aim is beauty or sublimity; if sublimity (power) is chosen, prioritize magnitude and abandon scattered or compromising ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single large 'thrust' (size or mass) is more effective than many small decorations. If choosing size, concentrate resources on achieving the necessary magnitude (one living figure should look less than life beside it). 'If he choose size, let him abandon decoration.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and visibility of bounding line
rubrics_metrics.description: To convey magnitude, a building should present one visible bounding line 'from top to bottom, and from end to end' so the eye can estimate its extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broken terminal lines (projecting cornices, recessed domes) destroy perceived majesty. For towers, location matters: central towers over a cross may lose apparent height; detached or west-end towers show height better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer true vertical or vertical with solemn projection for majesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Vertical bounding lines, or verticals with a measured projecting 'frown', convey nobler majesty than horizontal cornices or frivolous projection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projection should be dignified ('not a scowl') and the whole wall may 'nod' as well as 'frown'—examples: Palazzo Vecchio, Duomo of Florence, Doge's Palace projections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use broad surface (square/circle) to express power; use lines/elongation for division and grace
rubrics_metrics.description: When the aim is power and awfulness, choose broad, unbroken surfaces (square/circle plans); when the aim is grace or division, favor elongated forms and traced lines or arcades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface must be 'wide, bold and unbroken' to evoke sublimity; tracery and division (as in Flamboyant or Perpendicular styles) emphasize lines and delicate beauty. Material quality can affect the success of broad surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of primary forms according to purpose (square/circle vs elongated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the square or circle (and their solids) as elements of 'utmost power' for designs emphasizing surface, and elongated areas or series for designs emphasizing division or procession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Square and circle are pre-eminent for power; elongated series (arcades, ranges of columns) produce sublimity through repetition and multitudinous effect (example: Doge's palace as a model combining both).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose masonry honestly and choose masonry scale appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Masonry should generally be shown rather than concealed; the scale of the masonry should fit the building — smaller buildings need bolder masonry and large stones contribute to majesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disguise true fabric; the opposition of large stones or single-piece shafts to finer divided masonry gives noble character. Beware small, uniform stones making columns look like a 'close trellis' (example: facade of St. Madeleine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect material properties in finish and workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Finish and delicacy of workmanship should respond to the nature of the stone: marble invites smooth, delicate chiselling; granite or lava often better left roughly squared and 'granitic' in design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wasting labor polishing stones when the same resources could increase scale; there is dignity in the natural cleavage of stone. Choose finishing methods that suit material, purpose, and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose plan and massing to gather area for maximal surface effect
rubrics_metrics.description: To maximize the effect of surface (a source of power), arrange the building in forms that gather mass—a square or hollow square—and make surfaces broad and unified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Doge's palace (a hollow square) combines arcades to give length with large, unbroken upper surface, using color and pattern to enrich the plane without destroying breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition/continued series to create sublimity in elongated forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated elements (arcades, aisles, ranges of columns, repeated mouldings) can create a sense of sublimity in elongated forms by multiplicity rather than confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A continued series of marked features that the eye may be 'unable to number' gives sublimity (e.g., long arcades, Greek mouldings repeated). This expedient compensates for elongation when surface power is not primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of wall surfaces into masses of light/shade or linear tracery
rubrics_metrics.description: An architect must decide whether to divide wall surfaces by masses of light and shade (painting-like treatment) or by precise traced lines (incisions/projections) that read as linear composition at a distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the wall like a canvas with inherent sublimity; principles of relation of quantities are the same as in painting. Be cautious about breaking broad surfaces unnecessarily; divisions should obey quantity and grouping rules common to the arts.
